reasons.reader_question: Ittan's 'Hands go where they're sent' after 'Who sends the Keeper' points the reader at a sender above him, a specific gap. The muddled last line ('whose palm was open') blurs it slightly.
reasons.change: Ammu is buried, Neela leaves as a rogue with no master or ration, the kennels stay shut, and Ittan's unbroken step tells Devan the man knew he would be alive, with someone behind him.
reasons.romance_movement: The reason is new: the shared body ('I'll bleed in pairs'), his offer of a household ('I'd like it to have someone who is'), and her choice to keep her knee against his horse. It meets the beat's romance_change.
reasons.shown_chemistry: Attraction and care come through actions: he binds her wrists with his teeth, says 'I'll be here' on the step, orders the fodder cart, and his hand uncurls. Narration never claims chemistry.
reasons.character_logic: Mostly sound. Neela waters the animals but will not open the cages, Devan keeps Muthu at the gate, and Devan lets Ittan in unsearched. Devan's interior is the weak point: facing the man who paid for his death, he thinks only about evidence and never registers what Ittan meant for him or for Neela.
reasons.stakes_and_cost: Rogue status, the empty kennels, a crown record coming, and the sealing search tomorrow all carry cost. Muthu is held at the gate, so the next move tests a loyalty.
reasons.prose: Concrete and controlled, with no banned phrases and almost no AI tells. 'Twenty years, and it was a name' lands. Flaws: 'I can't give you your name, Kirri' reads as a slip, the closing hand metaphor is mixed, and two consecutive paragraphs open with 'She' ('She found Ammu' / 'She lay on her side').
reasons.continuity: Consistent with F224 (left ribs), F258/F265 (red lines on him), F235 (forty-one cages), F343, F207, F050, F149 and F407. 'She remembered a stable, and an order' sits close to F336 (the order was given in the passage) but can be read as the stable mention, so it does not conflict.

fixes: At 'They said you were poorly,' Ittan said, close now, and took Devan's hand: Stakes without depth. Devan is holding the hand that paid for his chamber and planned to take the widow's seal from Neela, but his interior goes straight to wax evidence. Ittan's 'And the bride?' is the natural moment. Add one or two short sentences of Devan's interiority: he knows what this man meant for her the morning after his death, and he chooses not to pull his hand away. Keep it restrained and literal, in his voice. This ties the plot escalation to Neela and lands the beat goal 'face the man who bought his death.'

At 'She did not cry again. There was none left to do it with.': internal contradiction. In the kennels she later 'wiped her face on the back of her wrapped wrist.' Either cut the face-wiping and have her wipe the bars or her hands, or change the grave line to 'She did not cry at the grave' so that the kennel tears read as the grief breaking through later.

At 'He stood very still and wondered whose palm was open.': the mixed metaphor muddies the reader question. Her closed hand, Ittan's 'hand', and an 'open palm' blur together. End on the plain question. For example, keep 'A hand went where it was sent,' then 'Then someone had sent it, and he knew of only one seal on the council that outranked the Keeper's.' Or simply 'Then whose was it?' Separately, in the kennels, change 'I can't give you your name, Kirri' to 'I can't give you back yourself, Kirri.' The original line reads as a slip, because Kirri is her name.
reader_question: If Ittan is only a hand sent to Kettamala, who sent him, and what will that power do when Devan opens the Keeper's cart tomorrow?
new_facts_assessment: F342r (fodder run timing, Muthu kept 'at the gate') is necessary and consistent with F393 and F217. F257r (Valli cloth shed at the cook-house corner) is plausible, since Ammu rode in as Valli (F236), and consistent, though the detail is optional. Several additions are unlisted and should be logged: Muthu held the arch against 'twelve men'; Chathu took his people and the ledger into the Blackbark Wood overnight; Vellan's track drags the ruined foreleg; Ittan's wife has had her cough three winters; Ittan's clerk carries a case of tallies; Devan says Janu is the only one at Kettamala who is his. None of these conflicts with canon. The twelve-men count and the clerk's tally case will bind later chapters, so they need recording.
